description: Why Blackman wrote the novel, why the RSC staged it, and the play's political resonance.
content_html:
Malorie Blackman: Writing for a Generation

Malorie Blackman OBE (born 1962) is a British author who served as Children’s Laureate from 2013 to 2015. She published Noughts & Crosses as a young adult novel in 2001, drawing on the speculative fiction tradition to construct an alternate Britain. Blackman has spoken in interviews about her motivation: she wanted young readers to understand racial inequality not through the dry facts of history but through the immediate experience of inhabiting a world where the hierarchy was reversed. The novel is addressed to a primarily young audience but was taken seriously by the wider literary world.

Blackman’s position as a British Black author writing about race in 2001 is part of the play’s context. The novel appeared two years after the Macpherson Report (1999), which found the Metropolitan Police institutionally racist following the inquiry into Stephen Lawrence’s murder. The novel’s alternate world is not escapism; it is a way of making British readers feel the weight of a racial hierarchy that existed, in a less inverted form, around them.

Key Fact

Malorie Blackman published the novel in 2001; Dominic Cooke’s RSC stage adaptation premiered in 2007 at the Civic Hall, Stratford-upon-Avon. The play was later toured by Pilot Theatre, including productions in 2019 and 2022. The set text for the exam is Cooke’s Nick Hern Modern Plays edition.

Dominic Cooke and the RSC Commission

Dominic Cooke (born 1966) is a British director who was Artistic Director of the Royal Court Theatre from 2007 to 2013. His RSC commission to adapt Noughts & Crosses for the stage was a significant institutional choice: the Royal Shakespeare Company bringing a young adult novel about racial injustice into its main programme signalled that the text was considered important beyond its original readership. Cooke’s previous work had engaged with political drama, and he brought to the adaptation a structural instinct for compression and clarity.

Cooke’s key decisions as adaptor were: to compress the novel’s sprawling narrative into a tight two-act structure; to foreground the dual-narrator device as the play’s central formal innovation; and to specify in the stage directions a design language of projection, soundscape and minimal staging rather than a naturalistic painted set. These are directorial and dramaturgical choices — not simply Blackman’s novel put on stage. Students must distinguish between what Blackman writes (the novel, the fictional world) and what Cooke stages (the theatrical form of the adaptation).

The RSC in 2007 was at a particular moment in its institutional history: attempting to widen its repertoire beyond the Shakespeare canon and to address its historically white audience demographics. Commissioning Cooke’s adaptation was part of a broader turn towards new writing and diverse voices. The play sits within a tradition of Black British theatre that includes writers like Tanika Gupta, debbie tucker green and Roy Williams — though Blackman came from a literary rather than theatrical background. The RSC premiere gave the adaptation the production values and reach of a major national company.

For a designer working on the play, this institutional context matters. The RSC’s Civic Hall, Stratford-upon-Avon, is a flexible space that can be configured in multiple ways. Cooke’s choice of a thrust stage for the original production meant that the direct-address narration sections — Sephy and Callum stepping forward to speak to the audience — had a physical intimacy that a proscenium configuration might not have achieved. The choice of staging configuration is always also a choice about the audience’s relationship to the story.

Historical and Social Context: Race in Britain at the Turn of the Century

The novel and its adaptation speak to a specific moment in British racial politics. The 1990s had seen the campaign for justice for Stephen Lawrence, a Black teenager murdered in a racially motivated attack in 1993 whose case exposed systematic failures in the police and legal system. The Macpherson Report (1999) named institutional racism as a structural problem, not a matter of individual prejudice. Blackman’s novel was written in the immediate aftermath of this inquiry, and the world of Noughts & Crosses — where noughts cannot access the same schools, face state violence, and are not believed by the legal system — is recognisably a transposed version of the experience the Macpherson Report documented.

There are also international reference points. The play’s world draws on the logic of apartheid South Africa (a legal racial hierarchy enforced by the state) and on US civil rights history (the segregated school as a site of political struggle). Blackman has been explicit that the novel is not set in any of these historical contexts, but that it is in dialogue with all of them. For a designer bringing the play to a contemporary audience, these resonances are an asset: the visual language of apartheid passes, of segregated schools, of state executions is legible without needing to be literal.

Key Fact

Key contexts for the play: the Macpherson Report (1999) on institutional racism in Britain following the Stephen Lawrence case; US civil rights history (segregated schooling, state violence); apartheid South Africa (legal racial hierarchy); and the tradition of Black British theatre engaging with race and empire.

Speculative Fiction as a Theatrical Form

The use of speculative fiction as the vehicle for political theatre is itself a meaningful choice. By setting the play in an alternate world, Blackman and Cooke create a distance from the specifics of any single historical racial injustice — which means the play can speak to multiple contexts without being trapped by any one of them. The audience is invited to do the intellectual work of translation: to notice where this invented world maps onto their own world, and where the mapping makes them uncomfortable.

This is related to Brecht’s concept of the Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect): by making the world strange — by flipping the racial hierarchy — Cooke’s adaptation prevents the audience from passively accepting the familiar. They cannot sit comfortably in a world they recognise. They must think. For a director, this means the staging should not strive for complete naturalistic illusion; the stylised elements of the design — the direct address, the projection, the minimal set — should maintain a productive distance between the audience and the fictional world, even while the intimate scenes between Sephy and Callum pull them close.

Some students treat the alternate-world setting as indicating that the play is set in a distant past or a far-off future, neither relevant to the present. This fundamentally misreads the play’s purpose. The alternate world is a mirror held up to the contemporary moment, not an escape from it. The play is explicitly set in a recognisable near-future Britain with contemporary technology, institutions and cultural references — the point is that the racial hierarchy feels natural and unremarkable to those at the top of it. That is the political argument. A director’s design choices — contemporary costume references, recognisable civic architecture in the set — should reinforce this proximity rather than push the story into a remote fantasy realm.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about context, the most common error is listing historical facts without connecting them to specific theatrical or staging choices. Context is not an essay of historical background — it is a justification for creative decisions. Use the formula: “Because the play was written in the aftermath of [historical context], a director/designer might choose [specific staging choice] to communicate [intended audience response].” For example: knowing that Blackman wrote in the shadow of the Macpherson Report on institutional racism helps justify a design choice that makes the state’s mechanisms — its schools, courts, prison officers — visually imposing and institutional rather than individual and domestic. Always connect context to a concrete design or performance interpretation.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Malorie Blackman published the novel in 2001 in the aftermath of the Macpherson Report on institutional racism. Dominic Cooke’s 2007 RSC stage adaptation compressed the novel into a two-act structure with dual narration, specifying a design language of projection, soundscape and minimal staging.
  • The play speaks to multiple historical contexts — British racial politics, US civil rights, apartheid South Africa — without being confined to any one. The alternate world is speculative fiction as political theatre: making the familiar strange so the audience must think rather than simply feel.
  • The Brechtian Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect) is relevant to Cooke’s adaptation: the stylised staging choices maintain a productive critical distance even while the intimate scenes draw the audience emotionally in. Context must always be translated into specific staging decisions for an exam answer to succeed.

practice_questions.text: In which year was Malorie Blackman's novel Noughts and Crosses first published?
Define the term 'Verfremdungseffekt' and explain how it applies to the staging of Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correct definition (Brecht's technique of making the familiar seem strange so the audience looks at it afresh rather than accepting it as natural; also called the alienation effect); 1 mark for a relevant application to the play (e.g. the racial reversal makes a recognisable hierarchy strange so the audience questions it rather than accepting it; the direct address and minimal staging maintain critical distance).

practice_questions.text: Explain how knowledge of the Macpherson Report (1999) might influence a set designer's choices for the state institutions — schools, courts, prison — in Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of what the Macpherson Report found (institutional racism as a structural problem) (1); explanation of how this context justifies a design choice that makes the state's spaces feel imposing and institutional rather than individual (e.g. elevated platforms, rigid architectural lines, harsh institutional lighting, uniforms with status markings) (1); explanation of the effect on the audience (the state feels systemic and impersonal, reinforcing the play's political argument) (1); link to a specific named space or moment in the play (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cooke's choice to use speculative fiction — an alternate Britain with a reversed racial hierarchy — shapes what a contemporary audience understands about racial privilege.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of what speculative fiction allows (distance from any single historical event; audience does the work of translation) (1); explanation of how the reversal makes privilege visible (those at the top do not see the system as a system) (1); reference to how this connects to the Verfremdungseffekt — making the familiar strange (1); link to a staging implication (e.g. contemporary design references keeping the world recognisably close rather than fantasy-remote) (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cooke uses the historical and social context of the play to make the audience engage with questions about racial inequality in contemporary Britain. Refer to at least two specific contextual factors and at least one staging or design choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies at least two specific contextual factors (Macpherson Report and institutional racism, US civil rights school segregation, apartheid South Africa, Black British theatre tradition) and connects each to a specific staging or design choice that makes the context legible in the production; analyses how Cooke uses the alternate world to create Brechtian distance while maintaining emotional engagement through the intimate scenes; discusses the dual role of the play as both a young adult story and a political intervention; reaches a judgement about what Cooke ultimately wants the audience to take away from the theatre.

Secure: Identifies at least two contexts; connects them to at least one staging choice; explains the intended audience response; reaches a general judgement.

Developing: Lists historical contexts without connecting them to staging or directorial choices; response is mostly background information rather than analysis of intention.

Emerging: Identifies one context with little analysis of how it shapes the play's theatrical meaning.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging Noughts and Crosses for a contemporary audience, discuss how you would use the play's speculative fiction setting to influence your design choices for costume, set and lighting. Refer to the historical and social contexts of the play and explain how your choices would communicate the themes of racial inequality and privilege to your audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a coherent directorial concept that uses the alternate-world setting as a design principle rather than a fantasy backdrop; specifies costume choices that communicate Cross privilege and nought marginalisation through recognisable contemporary markers (tailored versus worn, institutional uniform versus individual) rather than a simple black/white binary; names specific set elements that make state institutions feel imposing (raised levels, rigid lines, institutional materials such as steel or concrete for Cross spaces; lower, warmer, more worn materials for nought spaces); names specific lighting choices (e.g. warm directional light for Cross domestic spaces, harsher institutional fluorescent quality for state buildings); connects each choice to at least one historical or social context; explains the effect of each choice on the audience's understanding of privilege and inequality; response covers at least two design disciplines in depth and is anchored to named moments of the play.

Secure: Addresses multiple design disciplines; choices are mostly concrete; at least one historical context is connected to at least one design decision; effect on audience is explained.

Developing: Design choices are sometimes vague; historical context is mentioned but not connected to specific creative decisions; effect on audience is implied rather than argued.

Emerging: Identifies some design ideas without connecting them to context or explaining effects; response is largely descriptive.

What role did Malorie Blackman hold from 2013 to 2015?
Dominic Cooke's stage adaptation of Noughts and Crosses premiered at the _____ in 2007.
Brecht's term for making the familiar seem strange so the audience questions it is the _____ (alienation effect).

right: Named institutional racism as a structural problem in Britain
Provided the image of the segregated school as political battleground
Allowed Blackman to explore racial hierarchy through an alternate world

When did Dominic Cooke's RSC stage adaptation premiere?
What was Malorie Blackman's role from 2013 to 2015?
What did the Macpherson Report (1999) find?
flashcard_questions.a: That the Metropolitan Police was institutionally racist in its investigation of Stephen Lawrence's murder.
Fiction that imagines an alternate world or future to explore questions about the present.
Brecht's technique of making the familiar seem strange so the audience questions rather than accepts it.
Work by British playwrights of Black and Asian heritage engaging with histories of empire, migration and racial inequality.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Royal Shakespeare Company?
flashcard_questions.a: A major British theatre company known for ensemble productions of Shakespeare and new work, based in Stratford-upon-Avon.
A staging configuration in which the audience sits on three sides of the performance space.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a stylised approach in theatre design?
flashcard_questions.a: An approach that makes visible the play's artifice rather than creating complete naturalistic illusion.

flashcard_questions.q: Which two international historical contexts does the play's world draw on?
flashcard_questions.a: Apartheid South Africa (legal racial hierarchy) and US civil rights history (segregated schools).

flashcard_questions.q: What is Dominic Cooke's other major role in British theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: Artistic Director of the Royal Court Theatre, 2007–2013.

glossary_terms.definition: The genre of fiction that imagines how history might have developed differently if one or more key events had gone another way.
The 1999 public inquiry into the Metropolitan Police's handling of the racist murder of Stephen Lawrence, which concluded that the force was institutionally racist.
A major British theatre company founded in 1961, known for large-scale ensemble productions of Shakespeare and new work, based in Stratford-upon-Avon and London.
A body of work by British playwrights and practitioners of Black and Asian heritage, often engaging with the histories of empire, migration and racial inequality in Britain.
A staging configuration in which the audience sits on three sides of the performance space, with the stage extending into the auditorium.
The Brechtian technique of making the familiar seem strange, so that the audience looks at it afresh rather than accepting it as natural.
An approach to theatre that makes visible its own artifice, using techniques that remind the audience they are watching a constructed fiction.
